paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Heading and the Contrast between the Fool and the Seeker of God

easy.explanation: The heading identifies it as a Maschil of David.
easy.q: How is the psalm identified in its heading?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.”
easy.q: What does the fool say in his heart?

easy.explanation: God looked down from heaven upon “the children of men.”
easy.q: What did God look down from heaven upon?

answers: Someone who understood and sought God
medium.explanation: God looked to see whether there were any who understood and sought Him.
medium.q: What was God looking to find among the children of men?

medium.explanation: The word describes someone with understanding or discernment who seeks God.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “understood” most closely mean?

answers: The fool eats bread, while the other person does not
The fool is on earth, while the other person is in heaven
The fool denies God, while the other person seeks God
medium.explanation: The fool denies God, while God looks for someone who understands and seeks Him.
medium.q: What is the main contrast in these verses?

answers: It presents humanity’s condition from God’s viewpoint
It describes the journey of human beings
It explains how people eat bread
challenge.explanation: God’s view from heaven emphasizes His examination of humanity.
challenge.q: Why does the statement that God looked down from heaven strengthen the contrast in the passage?

challenge.explanation: The fool says this “in his heart,” pointing to his inner attitude.
challenge.q: Which phrase shows that the fool’s denial is an inward conviction rather than merely a public statement?

answers: Faith has no connection with conduct
The psalm distinguishes rejecting God from seeking Him
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts denial of God with understanding and seeking God.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from placing the fool opposite the person who seeks God?

paragraphs.title: The Corruption of the Generation and the Wicked’s Harm to the Good

answers: They are altogether corrupt and filthy
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Every one of them is gone back: they are altogether become filthy.”
easy.q: How are the people described in the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “there is none that doeth good, no, not one.”
easy.q: Is there anyone who does good according to the passage?

easy.explanation: They “eat up” God’s people as they eat bread.
easy.q: Whom do the workers of iniquity eat up?

answers: The people have turned aside, and the wicked harm them
The people rejoice, and the wicked praise them
The people pray, and the wicked join them
medium.explanation: The verses describe both widespread corruption and the wicked’s abuse of God’s people.
medium.q: What connection is made between the condition of the people and the actions of the wicked?

medium.explanation: The expression describes moral corruption and defilement.
medium.q: In this context, what does “become filthy” mean?

answers: They harm and exploit God’s people
medium.explanation: The forceful expression portrays the wicked as violently abusing the people.
medium.q: What does the phrase “eat up my people” suggest about the workers of iniquity?

challenge.explanation: “Every one” and “altogether” stress the broad extent of the corruption.
challenge.q: What emphasizes that the corruption described is widespread rather than limited to a few individuals?

answers: They combine moral violence with rejection of God
They are asking God for forgiveness
challenge.explanation: The passage joins their abuse of God’s people with the statement that they have not called upon God.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the wicked harming God’s people while not calling upon God?

answers: It emphasizes the absence of anyone doing good
It shows that many people seek God
challenge.explanation: The repeated wording intensifies the statement that no one does good, not even one.
challenge.q: Why is the repetition of “none” significant in these verses?

paragraphs.title: The Wicked’s Defeat and the Hope of Redemption

answers: It is fear where no fear was
It has nothing to do with the wicked
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “There were they in great fear, where no fear was.”
easy.q: What is revealed about the fear described in the passage?

answers: He appoints it as a leader
easy.explanation: God scatters the bones of him that encamps against His people.
easy.q: What does God do to the camp that encamps against His people?

answers: That Israel’s salvation would come out of Zion
That the wicked would receive more bread
easy.explanation: The psalm says, “Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion!”
easy.q: What does the psalm ask concerning Israel?

answers: Because God scattered and rejected the wicked
Because the fool changed his mind
medium.explanation: God defeats the opposing camp and puts it to shame, showing that the fear will not prevail.
medium.q: Why does the fear prove to be unfounded?

answers: The restoration and deliverance of God’s people
medium.explanation: The phrase expresses hope that God will restore and redeem His people.
medium.q: What does “bringeth back the captivity of his people” express in the context of the ending?

answers: Fear, victory for the wicked, and sorrow
The wicked’s defeat, hope of salvation, and Israel’s joy
Eating bread, prayer, and the people’s scattering
medium.explanation: The passage moves from the defeat of the wicked to salvation and the joy of Jacob and Israel.
medium.q: What is the main progression in these verses?

answers: Fear and the scattering of the wicked give way to hope and Israel’s joy
Prayer gives way to eating bread
Israel’s joy gives way to denial of God
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the defeat of the wicked to the hope and joy of God’s people.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between the two parts of the ending?

answers: It ends with hope and joy
It returns to the denial of God
It focuses on the strength of the wicked
challenge.explanation: These words show that the psalm ends with joyful hope for Jacob and Israel.
challenge.q: What do “rejoice” and “be glad” show about the ending of the psalm?

answers: The defeat of the wicked opens the way for the restoration and joy of God’s people
The defeat of the wicked prevents the people’s restoration
The verses make no connection between them
challenge.explanation: After describing the wicked’s defeat, the psalm expresses hope for Israel’s salvation and restoration.
challenge.q: How is Israel’s salvation connected with the defeat of the wicked?
